signals.title: Beam Turns Frontier-Scale Openness Into an Infrastructure Decision · Hugging Face Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Beam Turns Frontier-Scale Openness Into an Infrastructure Decision

Reflection's 501B-parameter Beam model pairs sparse expert routing with a one-million-token context window, but its real test is whether teams can turn open weights into an operable, measurable system.

Hugging Face Blog Editorial Editorial team · 6 min read

Announcement: October 16, 2026 Published: October 17, 2026

Source artwork · Hugging Face / credited contributors ↗

THE SHORT VERSION

Beam offers unusual scale and control, but successful adoption depends on testing the complete serving and agent system—not merely loading the checkpoint.

Reflection has released Beam, a text model aimed at coding and agentic workloads, under Apache 2.0. Its headline scale is 501 billion parameters, while sparse mixture-of-experts routing activates about 23 billion parameters for each token. The release also advertises a one-million-token context window and provides BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints. Support spans Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, alongside a separate Rust-based serving harness.

Those specifications make Beam interesting, but they do not make deployment simple. Sparse activation reduces arithmetic per token; it does not make the inactive experts disappear from memory. For engineering teams, the useful question is therefore not whether Beam behaves like a 23B model or a 501B model. It behaves like each in a different part of the system, and capacity planning has to respect both.

...

## An evaluation path before committing hardware

The release offers several serving routes, which makes staged evaluation possible. Begin with a hosted endpoint to test prompt formats, response parsing, and task quality. This stage should use a frozen test set with explicit pass criteria, including refusal and recovery cases.

Next, compare checkpoint precision on representative tasks. Quantization should be evaluated against application outcomes, not only generic benchmarks. Track structured-output validity, tool-selection accuracy, long-context retrieval, latency percentiles, and cost per successful task. Small aggregate benchmark differences can conceal a material regression in one critical workflow.

Only then should a team reproduce the expected concurrency and context distribution on the intended hardware. Include cold starts, burst traffic, and degraded-node scenarios. This sequence keeps the biggest infrastructure decision until there is evidence that Beam solves the actual problem.

signals.excerpt:
# ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars

OpenViking from ByteDance's Volcengine treats agent memory, knowledge and skills as a virtual filesystem, crossing 40,000 GitHub stars.

 By Marcello Babbili · AI-assisted newsroom October 19, 2026 3 min read 

Image generated by OpenAI

ByteDance's Volcengine team published OpenViking, an open-source context database that treats everything an AI agent knows as files under a `viking://` filesystem, and the project crossed 40,000 stars on GitHub this week after gaining 105 stars in a single day on the platform's trending list S¹.

The approach challenges how most agent builders work today: stitching together separate systems for retrieval-augmented generation (the standard method for feeding documents into a model), conversation memory, and tool or skill management. OpenViking collapses all three into one virtual filesystem that an agent can browse and read on demand P² P⁴.

...

My read: This is the first agent-memory project I've seen that refuses to separate knowledge from memory from skills at the storage layer. Most teams I watch are still gluing a vector database to a chat-history buffer and calling it done. The filesystem metaphor is elegant, but the benchmark numbers are entirely self-reported and nobody outside the Volcengine team has verified them. I'd want to see independent tau2-bench results before believing the performance claims, and the 40,000-star count tells me about GitHub momentum, not production readiness.

...

### One filesystem, three context types

The Viking team, part of ByteDance's cloud infrastructure arm Volcengine, organises context into three types: resources for reference material, memories for information retained from interactions, and skills for task procedures P⁴. Each piece of context loads in three tiers: L0, a one-sentence abstract; L1, a core overview; and L2, the full original data S¹. An agent scans the L0 summaries to decide what it needs, then drills down to L2 only for relevant items, which keeps token consumption down.

When a conversation session ends, OpenViking commits and archives it as Markdown files that a developer can read and edit by hand S¹. Memories sit in readable text, not a binary store, which makes debugging and correction straightforward.

...

### The benchmarks nobody has checked

The project reports evaluation results on two benchmarks: LoCoMo, which tests long-conversation user memory, and tau2-bench, which tests multi-turn agent tasks S¹. Version 0.3.22 used Doubao 2.0 Pro, Volcengine's own vision-language model, for the memory evaluation S¹. These results are self-reported. The repository does not include peer-reviewed or third-party-audited benchmark data, and the README is the maintainers' description of their own work, not an independent review.

A developer who wants to try the system without committing to an install can use OpenViking Studio, a browser-based demo that requires no setup S¹.

The repository is written primarily in Python and carries the volcengine organisation label on GitHub, though the about page confirms the team sits inside ByteDance's Volcengine unit P².

Until an independent team reproduces the LoCoMo or tau2-bench results, the 40,000-star count measures interest, not proof.

# Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model

October 19, 2026

## Abstract

We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

signals.excerpt:
# Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API

OCT. 19, 2026

 Ping Yu Staff Software Engineer 

 Quentin Khan Sr. Software Engineer 

 Chintan Parikh Sr. Product Manager 

 Lu Wang Sr. Staff Software Engineer 

Shipping on-device AI means meeting tight latency and memory budgets on every device you target. The most common path for deploying models in production is converting a trained model, for example converting a PyTorch model with LiteRT Torch, and running it with the LiteRT runtime. This offers the quickest and most reliable route to production, and it's the path we recommend for most projects. Sometimes, though, developers want full control over how a network is represented and optimized to support new architectures or to try a new lowering logic without waiting for upstream framework updates.

For ultimate control, developers write computations manually in native C++ or shader languages. Apple's MLX made this code-first approach popular on Apple silicon, and llama.cpp showed how far tailored C++ implementations can take LLM inference. However, the level of control comes at a significant cost: implementations are tightly coupled to specific backends (such as Metal, OpenCL, or Vulkan) and must be rewritten for each new hardware target. Furthermore, managing zero-copy buffer interoperability and synchronization across CPU, GPU, and NPU, while gluing together pre-processing, inference, and post-processing, demands substantial manual engineering effort.

To solve the above challenges, we are excited to announce the release of the novel LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight authoring layer in the LiteRT stack, designed to improve handcrafting models. It combines the flexibility of native authoring with cross-platform portability. You build the computation graph op by op in C++, choosing exactly which ops run and how they connect. The same graph can run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU (powered by open-source ML Drift) and NPU, or without model file or runtime directly on CPU through XNNPACK, so you don't rewrite it for each new hardware target. Model inference and pre/post-processing can be assembled with the same API and chained through shared accelerator buffers, so that data never round-trips through the CPU. Start with the conversion path, which remains the best default for most models. Reach for the Tensor API when you need low-level control over the graph or want the whole pipeline to run end to end on the accelerator.

The LiteRT Tensor API also serves as an ideal programmatic foundation for AI coding agents, providing structured primitives to generate, rewire, and tune model graphs automatically. In the rest of this post, we’ll dive into the design and walk through practical code examples showing how to author models from scratch.

...

To show the Tensor API in practice, we built an interactive Segment Anything App, running entirely on-device in the browser on WebGPU. The app enables real-time multi-object segmentation and tracking via Meta's Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2), triggered either by simple clicks or natural language prompts powered by Gemma 4 E2B.

The SAM 2 model is fully authored in C++ via the LiteRT Tensor API. A coding agent wrote and evolved it from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU. See that the complete implementation and the web app are open source in the LiteRT Samples GitHub repo.

...

## Cross-platform performance

We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder). The SAM 2.1 sample includes the benchmark commands so you can reproduce the results.

 Note: Times cover the image encoder and mask decoder; pre- and post-processing add ~0.34 ms. Output masks match Meta's PyTorch reference pixel for pixel.

signals.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands Beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
Oct 19, 2026 2 min read 

by

- Sergio De Simone 

Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment.

> Designed to run on consumer hardware such as mobile devices and laptops, EmbeddingGemma 2 delivers low-latency semantic representations for on-device applications, like search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), classification, and clustering.

Thanks to its multimodal capabilities, EmbeddingGemma 2 supports a wide range of retrieval tasks, including finding relevant documents, screenshots, and recordings in response to a query, searching source code using natural language, and retrieving video content based on textual descriptions.

EmbeddingGemma 2's key feature, Google says, is its ability to represent text, code, images, video, and audio in a unified 768-dimensional embedding space. This enables developers to build retrieval systems that search across different media types without maintaining separate, incompatible embedding spaces for different media types.

> Despite coming from different modalities, the embeddings generated by EmbeddingGemma 2 occupy the same dimensional space and can be compared on their semantic similarity.

The model allows developers to load only the encoders required for their applications, scaling from 270 million parameters for text and code to 740 million for full multimodal support. According to Google, the model "significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search".

...

EmbeddingGemma 2 supports Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), which allows embeddings to be truncated into shorter, unit-length vectors, reducing storage requirements. For example, storing a million 768-dimensional vectors at bfloat16 precision takes roughly 1.5 GB of memory, while truncating them to 128 dimensions requires just 250 MB, bringing a sixfold reduction. However, this implies a retrieval quality trade-off. Google therefore recommends using truncation only when storage or search speed require it. At 128 dimensions, the model retains approximately 90% of quality with text, but performance drops to around 75% for image, video, and speech retrieval.

...

EmbeddingGemma was introduced last year with a focus on "offline and privacy-sensitive scenarios, such as searching across personal files locally, running mobile RAG pipelines with Gemma 3n, or building domain-specific chatbots". EmbeddingGemma 2 is available on Hugging Face.

signals.excerpt:
### Reflection AI open-sources Beam’s weights, post-training recipes

 by Maria Deutscher 

Startup Reflection AI Inc. today made the weights of Beam, its first large language model, available on Hugging Face.

The company also released technical resources that will enable developers to customize the algorithm.

Originally introduced last week, Beam is one of the industry’s most advanced open-source LLMs. It features about 500 billion parameters, yet approaches the performance of models four times its size on some benchmarks. It also uses significantly less computing power and memory.

Reflection AI trained Beam over two months using several thousand high-end graphics cards. Such large-scale training runs are prone to errors that can decrease model quality. According to Reflection AI, its engineers addressed the challenge by developing a set of custom reliability optimization algorithms.

...

Beam’s newly released weights are available in multiple versions. There’s a standard edition and several scaled-down variants that keep information in smaller units of data. That arrangement, which is known as quantization, trades off some output quality for increased hardware efficiency.

The weights are available alongside training recipes, code templates that enable users to fine-tune the model. A vibe coding startup, for example, could create a fine-tuning workflow that enhances the model’s programming capabilities. The recipes are joined by tools that can be used to measure how customizations change Beam’s capabilities and safety guardrails.

...

Reflection AI has also released a drafter model for Beam. It can be used to implement speculative decoding, an inference approach designed to lower hardware usage. The basic idea behind the method is to use a lightweight LLM, the drafter model, to generate the initial version of a prompt response. Beam checks the output for errors before displaying it to the user.

Performing inference in a hardware-efficient manner requires developers to use a software tool called a serving engine. Adapting an LLM to a given serving engine can involve a significant amount of work. 

Today’s release includes ready-to-use Beam configurations for several popular serving engines. Developers also have access to fused kernels, code snippets that compress multiple inference calculations into a single operation to speed up processing.

signals.excerpt:
AI & Compute roundup: Hugging Face runs Meta’s 816B open model at 18 tokens a second on one 512GB Mac

# AI & Compute roundup: Hugging Face runs Meta’s 816B open model at 18 tokens a second on one 512GB Mac

Hugging Face ran Meta's 816B Muse Spark Open at 2-bit on one 512GB M3 Ultra Mac. Reflection's 501B Beam needs about 280 GB at 4-bit, and NVIDIA's Bolt 74B-A9B is built to fit 24GB.

October 19, 2026 · AI & Compute · 3 minute read · Saeid Yazdani

Two frontier-scale open-weight models landed a day apart, and both are mixture-of-experts designs: memory follows the total parameter count, while speed follows the few parameters active for each token. The second memory bill, the cache that grows with context, is where the two differ by roughly a factor of seven.

### Meta’s Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters and runs on a 512GB Mac at 2-bit

Muse Spark Open has about 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion of them active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens, according to Hugging Face’s launch post for the model. It takes text, images, audio and video and writes text. All 256 experts in each layer stay in memory while eight run per token, which puts the BF16 checkpoint at about 1.5 TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint is the 4-bit option for Blackwell GPUs: the post runs it on a single B200 node in transformers and on four GB300 GPUs in the SGLang reference setup, and its Inference Endpoints recipe uses eight RTX Pro 6000 cards with a context length of 131072 tokens.

The numbers a home lab can use come from Apple hardware. On an M3 Ultra with 512GB, an imatrix-calibrated 2-bit llama.cpp quantization uses 304 GB and generates 18 tokens a second. An oMLX 3-bit quantization takes about 344 GB and generates 21 tokens a second after a 1024-token prompt, with prompt processing at 225 tokens a second.

Context is where that Mac runs out of room. The post puts the BF16 cache at about 250 KB per token, or about 266 GB for a full million-token window. Added to the 304 GB of 2-bit weights, one full-length sequence would need about 570 GB, which is more than the machine has unless the cache is quantized too. That sum is our arithmetic from the post’s figures.

...

### Reflection’s Beam is a 501B Apache 2.0 model that needs about 280 GB at 4-bit

Beam is the first model from Reflection, a new US lab, and Hugging Face’s post describes it as a text-only model for coding and agent workflows with 501 billion parameters, 23 billion active per token, a one-million-token window and an Apache 2.0 license. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB. NVFP4 shrinks it to roughly 280 GB but needs Blackwell, so FP8 checkpoints cover Hopper and Ampere cards. Two B200s with 180 GB each can hold the weights and little else, so the post recommends four, with a full 8xB200 node, two B300s at 288 GB each or 8xRTX Pro 6000 as alternatives.

The cache is the smaller bill here. Only 9 of Beam’s 52 layers attend to the whole sequence, and the other 43 keep a 512-token sliding window, so the cache grows by about 36 KiB per token and reaches 36.08 GiB at one million tokens in BF16. That is roughly a seventh of Muse Spark Open’s 266 GB. Each layer caches the same 2,048 values per token in both models, so the gap comes from Muse Spark Open keeping 62 full-length layers against Beam’s 9.

Reflection’s benchmark table, reproduced in the post, shows little cost from quantization. SWEBench Verified reads 81.6% in BF16, 80.2% in FP8 and 80.7% in NVFP4. Terminal Bench v2.1 reads 80.1%, 78.9% and 78.2%.

...

### NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B is built to fit in 24GB

At the other end, NVIDIA’s announcement presents Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB as a model for local agent harnesses on RTX/DGX Spark. It uses native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and leave room for other applications, and it is available now. NVIDIA ranks it first among open models in its class on PinchBench and second on BrowseComp. Bolt E4B 4GB, for GeForce RTX, Jetson and RTX/DGX Spark, follows on

### Microsoft Foundry Update Brings Scheduled AI Agents, Smarter Tool Use and GPT-6 Models

- By David Ramel
- 10/19/2026

### Key Takeaways

- Microsoft Foundry Routines and Tool Search are now generally available, enabling scheduled AI agent execution and on-demand tool discovery.
- A new Insights preview helps developers troubleshoot agent behavior, while Model Router adds controls for model consistency and routing visibility.
- Microsoft expanded its GPT-6 model lineup with new pricing options and added bring-your-own-model support in Foundry Local 2.1.

Microsoft is making its Foundry AI development platform more useful for building and running autonomous agents, adding capabilities for scheduling work, finding tools on demand and figuring out what went wrong when agents don't behave as expected.

Those are among the highlights of Microsoft's September 2026 Foundry roundup, published Oct. 15, which also covers an expanded GPT-6 model lineup, new voice and agent resilience capabilities, and updates to local AI development tools.

Much of the attention goes to making agents more useful after developers have built them -- automating their execution, reducing the overhead of tool definitions and providing better ways to investigate their behavior.

...

Putting AI Agents to Work on a Schedule One of the bigger changes is the general availability of Routines, which let developers trigger agents automatically without having to set up a separate scheduling system.

Routines can start an agent on a timer, a recurring schedule, or supported events involving GitHub issues and Microsoft Teams channels. Configuration, identity and execution history are managed within the Foundry project.

For example, a developer could have an agent automatically collect GitHub changes every Monday, prepare release notes and pass the results along for review.

 [Click on image for larger view.] Scheduled Agents Create Developer Changelog Reports (source: Microsoft).

Microsoft's example uses two hosted agents, one built with the GitHub Copilot SDK to collect source material and another using Microsoft Agent Framework to prepare the resulting changelog for delivery to Teams.

...

Microsoft cautions that Routines aren't a replacement for multi-agent orchestration or approval workflows. They start the work, but developers still need to handle what happens afterward, including reviewing results and delivering them to the right destination.

...

Smarter Tool Use and Better Agent Troubleshooting Another generally available feature, Tool Search, tackles a familiar problem with tool-heavy AI agents: loading large numbers of tool definitions into the model's context even when only a few are needed.

Instead, agents can discover available tools and load their definitions on demand through Foundry Toolboxes, potentially reducing input-token costs and leaving more context available for the actual task.

Tool Search is generally available, while support for Toolboxes in prompt agents remains in public preview. Agent-to-Agent (A2A) capabilities also reached general availability.

...

Meanwhile, the new Insights capability, now in public preview, aims to help developers understand why an agent isn't performing well.

Insights examines agent traces and groups recurring behavior into findings, including supporting evidence, likely causes and suggested improvements. Microsoft's examples include repeated oversized prompts, unnecessary retries after rate-limit errors and problems confirming task delivery.

...

More GPT-6 Choices, with Big Pricing Differences On the model side, Microsoft expanded Foundry's GPT-6 offerings with three generally available models targeting different performance and cost requirements: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

Astra targets demanding workloads, while Sol offers performance closer to Astra at a lower price. Luna is positioned as an efficient option for focused, high-volume tasks.

...

All three models support context windows of approximately 1.05 million tokens, with up to 128,000 output tokens, including reasoning tokens.

...

Model Router, which selects models for requests, gained preview support for session affinity and routing metadata. Session affinity lets related requests preferentially use the same eligible model, potentially improving prompt-cache reuse, although Microsoft says neither cache hits nor model consistency are guaranteed.

...

The routing metadata provides more visibility into which models are selected and when fallback occurs.

...

Foundry Local Gets Bring-Your-Own-Model Support Developers working with local AI models also get new capabilities in Foundry Local 2.1, released Sept. 30.

The update lets developers register compatible ONNX Runtime GenAI models without having to copy or transfer the underlying model files. Bring-your-own-model support is available across C++, C#, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript and Rust.

Other improvements include custom text tools, better cancellation handling, token accounting and accessibility improvements to the model browser.

Microsoft also released a preview Content Understanding Toolkit and command-line interface (CLI) for working with analyzers and local files, along with updates to its speech recognition tools.

More Tools for Developers The September updates also cover changes to the development experience, including a new Foundry Dev Pack installer intended to simplify environment setup.

For Visual Studio Code users, the Foundry Toolkit gained solution templates, skill-only Toolboxes, and controls for steering or stopping active Responses work, along with reconnection support for unfinished background responses.

signals.excerpt:
By Kyle Belmonte Published: Oct 19 2026, 1:04 PM EDT

 Kirill KUDRYAVTSEV/AFP via Getty Images 

Tencent's Hunyuan research team released Hy-Memory-30B-A3B on October 15 under the Apache 2.0 license — a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model whose entire job is deciding what an AI agent should remember Hy-Memory-30B-A3B on Hugging Face. On four proprietary memory benchmarks designed and run by Tencent, it scored a macro average of 55.49 against Claude Opus 5's 54.62 — a 0.87-point margin that the company is calling a lead over Anthropic's flagship arXiv benchmark comparison paper.

Those benchmarks have not been independently replicated, and the word to use here is "claims." What is independently verifiable is that the model exists, ships free and open-weight, and is the first purpose-trained open-source system targeting the memory-write path specifically —a bottleneck that matters for every developer building agents that need to remember things across sessions.

The release landed with unusual completeness for a first-day open-source drop: model weights on Hugging Face, a Python SDK on PyPI, a technical paper on arXiv, and a macOS desktop aggregation application called MemHub with binary installers published the following day Hy-Memory GitHub repository.

...

### Benchmark Numbers — and Why "Claims" Is the Right Word

On four memory evaluation harnesses — Mem0, Hy-Memory, MemOS, and EverMemOS — Hy-Memory-30B-A3B posted per-harness scores of 54.02, 60.55, 50.51, and 56.89, yielding a macro average of 55.49 Tencent's published benchmark results. Claude Opus 5 scored 54.62 overall. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash followed at 53.64. Qwen3-30B-A3B — a model with a similar active-parameter count but no memory specialization — scored 44.37. Evaluations used 20 percent fixed subsamples of each benchmark.

The EverMemOS result is the benchmark figure Tencent presents as its strongest evidence of generalization. The team describes EverMemOS as a held-out harness, one the model was not explicitly trained against Tencent's published benchmark results. If accurate, a held-out evaluation reduces (but does not eliminate) the risk of benchmark-specific optimization.

What the held-out framing does not change: Tencent designed all four harnesses, selected the subsamples, and ran all evaluations. No independent lab has replicated these results as of this publication. The 0.87-point margin over Claude Opus 5 is the kind of figure that can shift substantially under different evaluation parameters. Benchmark categories for agent memory are an emerging field without standardized methodology; the frameworks used here were all developed or shaped by teams in the same research ecosystem.

signals.title: Georgia Tech, Nvidia, Stanford Boost LLM Inference Throughput — Die Signal
signals.excerpt:
# Georgia Tech, Nvidia, Stanford Boost LLM Inference via Memory

Georgia Tech, Nvidia and Stanford let GPUs read HBM and host DRAM at the same time, raising LLM inference throughput on existing accelerators.

3nm

Operator

Amara Osei

## Spec summary

1. S01 Georgia Tech, Nvidia and Stanford jointly published the research.
2. S02 The method improves LLM inference throughput by accessing HBM and host memory concurrently.
3. S03 It targets models whose weights and key-value caches exceed a single GPU's HBM capacity.
4. S04 Nvidia's participation links the work to its H100, H200 and B200 accelerator lines.
5. S05 The approach treats host DRAM as a working memory tier instead of an overflow store.

...

Researchers at Georgia Tech, Nvidia and Stanford have published a method that raises large language model inference throughput by letting accelerators access high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and host DRAM concurrently, rather than treating host memory as an overflow tier used only when HBM fills up.

The work targets a structural bottleneck in LLM deployment. Model weights and key-value caches have outgrown the HBM capacity of single accelerators, which forces operators to shard models across GPUs or offload tensors to host memory in sequential, blocking transfers. Both paths cost time.

...

## What does the technique change?

The paper's core move is scheduling. Instead of staging data from host DRAM into HBM before the compute units can touch it, the system overlaps reads from both pools during inference.

That shifts host memory from a fallback store into a working tier. The GPU draws on PCIe- or CXL-attached DRAM while it continues to stream from HBM, so the compute engines stall less often waiting for a transfer to finish.

The practical consequence: models that exceed local HBM can run on fewer accelerators, or serve more requests per second on the same hardware.

...

Three institutions appear on the work: Georgia Tech, Stanford and Nvidia. Nvidia's involvement signals vendor interest, since the company sells the HBM-equipped GPUs — H100 with 80 GB, H200 with 141 GB, B200 above that — whose capacity limits the technique addresses.

Capacity pressure keeps rising. Frontier-class LLMs now reach hundreds of gigabytes of weights, and key-value caches grow with context length and concurrent users. Memory, not floating-point throughput, increasingly sets the serving ceiling.

signals.title: NVIDIA Releases Dory, a 4B Model With Adjustable Inference Depth | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA Releases Dory, a 4B Model With Adjustable Inference Depth

NVIDIA’s Dory1.0-4B lets developers adjust inference depth by running a shared block of layers one to four times, trading compute for accuracy. Its benchmark results show gains on some coding tasks as loop count rises, while other scores fl

AI.info Team · Written with AI · fact-checked · 2026-10-17

NVIDIA’s Dory1.0-4B offers developers a choice: spend more inference compute on a response without loading a larger model, or keep the model to a single pass for lower compute per token. The company’s own benchmark table shows the trade-off is uneven. On SWE-bench Verified, Dory scores rise from 50.3 at one loop to 61.8 at four; on GPQA Diamond, the score rises from 69.19 to 72.41 at two loops, then slips to 72.16 at four.

NVIDIA dated the release October 16, 2026, on its Hugging Face model card. The checkpoint has 4 billion parameters and supports up to 262,144 tokens of context in NVIDIA’s BF16 launch configuration. Rather than increasing its parameter count, Dory repeatedly applies the same 20-layer block between an eight-layer input block and an eight-layer output block.

...

A shared block sets Dory’s depth

The model uses a looped, or latent-recurrent, normalized-GPT architecture with sliding-window and full-attention layers. At inference, developers can set the shared block to run one, two, three or four times. NVIDIA recommends two loops as a starting point, describing one loop as an option when reducing compute per token matters most and four as an option when additional accuracy is worth the cost, particularly for agentic tasks.

Repeated computation takes place in the model’s latent representations rather than requiring longer generated answers, according to the card. NVIDIA says looping can reduce the number of output tokens needed to solve a task, but also advises developers to evaluate end-to-end latency and cost on their own workloads. The benchmark scores alone do not establish whether extra loops make a particular application faster or cheaper overall.

...

## Coding gains come with uneven scores

The clearest gain in NVIDIA’s table appears on coding and agent benchmarks. Dory’s SWE-bench Verified score climbs from 50.3 at one loop to 59.5 at two and 61.8 at four. At four loops, that is above the listed 54.7 for Qwen3.5-4B and 61.0 for Qwen3.5-9B.

Other results temper that comparison. On GPQA Diamond, Dory’s four-loop score of 72.16 trails the listed scores for Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B; the model’s four-loop Humanity’s Last Exam score is 10.43, compared with 11.31 for Qwen3.5-4B. NVIDIA says it measured accuracy using a consistent evaluation harness, but flags its Artificial Analysis v4.3.2 estimates as internal results that may differ from official scores.

...

The release comes in BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4 and Q5_K_M GGUF formats. The GGUF download is a quantized export sized at about 3.67 GB. NVIDIA’s setup guide says the benchmark results are for BF16, not the downloadable GGUF file. Its setup guide also says llama.cpp support is still awaiting inclusion in a release, and directs users to a Dory-enabled build in the meantime.

# DeepSeek Opens Its In-House Search Engine To Developers 

- DeepSeek opened its in-house search engine to developers and says it filters GEO manipulation.
- Each result includes an authority tier for the page and a relevance score.
- Site: queries return some of your indexed pages along with each page's authority tier.

A Chinese AI lab opened its search engine to developers. Each result carries a page-level authority tier, and DeepSeek says it filters GEO manipulation.

SEJ STAFF Matt G. Southern

...

- 1 hour ago 
- ⋅
- 4 min read

...

SEJ STAFF Matt G. Southern Senior News Writer at Search Engine Journal

 Bio 

DeepSeek opened its in-house search engine to developers on Oct. 17, and the company’s changelog says the engine filters SEO spam, “GEO manipulation,” and low-quality AI-generated content.

Each result from the new Search API includes an authority tier for the page and a relevance score, and the API accepts site: queries that limit results to one domain.

...

DeepSeek’s changelog says its in-house engine handles search on its website and in its API, indexes hundreds of billions of web pages, and takes in hundreds of millions of search requests a day from around the world.

GEO (generative engine optimization) is when you shape your content to be cited by AI answer engines. DeepSeek’s changelog states that they credit strict detection as the source of filtering; however, it has not defined what GEO manipulation is or described how their detection process operates. On May 15, Google said “our spam policies also apply to generative AI responses in Google Search.”

...

The privacy policy of

...

## What The Search API Returns

Each Search API result contains an authority field; authority fields range from 0 to 4 with -1 being unknown. According to DeepSeek’s API reference, pages with tiers of 3+ are described as “highly authoritative” sources.

The rerank score (another field) is a scale of 0-3 and incorporates signals that include relevance, authority and freshness. A rerank score of 1.5+ is considered high quality. The guide and the reference do not explain how a page receives its tier or score.

Each result also comes with a snippet for display, typically 100 to 200 characters, and a summary meant for a model to read, typically 600 to 800 characters. Page content comes back too when a request asks for it and the content is available. Queries can be limited with site: and filtered by language and date published.

Search and Fetch each cost $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests. Searches that return no results aren’t billed, and requesting 50 results costs the same as requesting just one.

...

DeepSeek’s Fetch API was released with Search. Fetch provides a single Markdown page and “is subject to the target site’s availability and access policies,” as per the guide.

...

According to the EU summary of the data used to train DeepSeek-V4, the crawler is “designed to respect robots.txt instructions and other standard web protocols, where applicable.” However, the summary does not identify which crawler this refers to.

...

Additionally, none of the launch pages (the guide, API references, changelog and announcement) provide identification of a crawler for the search index nor do they provide information on what user agent Fetch uses.

...

In addition to providing information about several crawlers, the Known Agents bot directory lists a DeepSeekBot user agent and describes it as an AI training data crawler.

...

## Looking Ahead

If you use Claude Code, Codex, or DeepSeek Harness with the DeepSeek API, your server-side searches and page fetches are already handled through the Search and Fetch APIs at no cost. Billing for these server-side calls will begin on Oct. 31 at 16:00 UTC (noon ET).

signals.title: Crusoe Keeps 4-Bit Weights to Cut LoRA Memory by 75% | StartupHub.ai
signals.excerpt:
# Crusoe Keeps 4-Bit Weights to Cut LoRA Memory by 75%

Crusoe shows how storing frozen base weights in 4-bit and dequantizing in-kernel cuts LoRA memory by up to 75% without accuracy loss.

StartupHub.ai Staff Oct 17 at 1:17 PM 2 min read

Crusoe keeps base weights in 4-bit and dequantizes inside the kernel· Crusoe Blog

Crusoe Blog says its post-training team built LoRA training that keeps frozen base weights in 4-bit and dequantizes them inside the kernel.

LoRA, or Low-Rank Adaptation, freezes the base model and trains two small matrices that add about one percent of parameters.

A 1 trillion parameter model like Kimi-K2.6 needs at least 2 terabytes for base weights in bf16, or four HGX H100 nodes, according to Crusoe.

In unmerged LoRA inference Crusoe keeps the base path in mxfp4 with activations quantized to mxfp8 while the adapter path stays in bf16.

On Blackwell the matmul runs natively in mxfp4, but on Hopper Crusoe still stores 4-bit and dequantizes to bf16 inside the kernel.

In the backward pass Crusoe needs only gradients for A, B and the input, so frozen W never needs a bf16 copy or optimizer update.

DeepSeek V4 also cuts single-token FLOPs and KV cache to about ten percent of DeepSeek V3.2 at one million tokens, per Codersera's setup guide.

Crusoe reports no accuracy drop from the train-inference precision mismatch, but the result relies on the quantization passthrough assumption used in quantization-aware training.

Serverless Fine-Tuning with this dequant-on-the-fly kernel is now generally available in Crusoe Intelligence Foundry and bills per training token.

signals.title: NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes

 Erik Dunteman Oct 19, 2026 

# NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes

Last week, NVIDIA hand-delivered Modal’s first Vera CPU server to our SF office. It’s now purring away in a server rack, and we’re pretty excited about what it could mean for Modal Sandboxes and, consequently, Modal users.

Vera is NVIDIA’s new Arm-compatible CPU, built for the Vera Rubin GPU platform but also available as a standalone CPU server.

Supporting Arm would be a huge change for Modal, coming from a long history exclusively running x86 machines. We’d need to make changes across our infrastructure and image build system to support an entirely different CPU architecture, but the benchmarks are impressive: a 2x increase on throughput. With this, the NVIDIA Vera CPU becomes an incredibly compelling option for powering Modal Sandboxes.

...

## Benchmarking the Vera CPU

To test Vera, we built a set of representative workloads and benchmarks for agentic Sandboxes.

Creating an “agentic” benchmark is a challenging task, given most of the work done on the servers is not CPU bound, and there’s no specific dimension we’d want to optimize for. Where a DB workload could optimize for disk I/O and an image processing workload could optimize SIMD, for sandboxes we needed to come up with a simulator that is both concurrent and heterogeneous: a big ol’ bag of chaos we could throw at the CPU.

From this we developed Agentless Agent Bench, a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers, stripped of all network calls and prewarmed in concurrent Docker containers, isolating just the tasks actually performed on the CPU by agents and RL - compilation, file grepping, git operations, device emulation, and more.

Running the benchmark shows us both linear task completion time, and concurrent throughput metrics.

Below are results showing per-task latency for a selection of Terminal-Bench tasks you’d reasonably see an agent running in your sandboxes. This experiment was run on a machine without load, serially, so the results show pure straightline latency.

 

Seeing these results first, I was admittedly skeptical. Across the 50 tasks we benchmarked, Vera often performed better than the other CPUs, but not always, and not by a particularly large margin.

But straightline latency on a quiet host isn’t what Sandbox users experience. In practice, hundreds of workloads are competing for resources at once. Moving onward to testing under load, we get an entirely different story for Vera.

...

## Vera gets better under heavy load

Agentless Agent Bench has a test for throughput, in which it increases the count of concurrent containers running on the machine, looping as many task completions as possible in a fixed time.

Counterintuitively, Vera gets better under heavy load.

During one of our onsites at NVIDIA HQ, I vividly remember first seeing these results, and being unable to believe how they could be true.

Our early benchmarking runs show up to double the task throughput on Vera compared with an equivalent x86 GNR machine, despite individual task latency measuring equal to, or sometimes even lower than, the x86 machine. This is because Vera does not slow down as jobs accumulate but rips through each one at the original pace.

When asked, the Vera team confirmed that these results are not surprising. It was at this moment I became a Vera believer.

...

## The killer feature is contention

Vera’s killer feature is the ability to hold up under contention. Its high memory bandwidth allows for significantly more container workloads to pack per core, without CPU throttling - which explains why Vera pulls so far ahead of the alternatives in our benchmarks.

At added CPU counts, the alternatives hit early throughput plateaus, while Vera continues to improve, suggesting we could push it even further than the node we had access to for benchmarking.

For Modal, this unlocks greater packing density and more forgiving burst protection.

For Sandbox users, we can offer higher absolute scale and throughput, without sacrificing latency.

We’re very excited to roll out support for Vera CPUs to power Modal Sandboxes, and work closely with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale up our fleet.

signals.excerpt:
between agent turns

Blockway has released new Agens Volundr weights aimed at extended sessions with AI agents. A continuation feature reuses the state from earlier input when a conversation resumes, leaving subsequent requests to process the added messages. The design uses both growing memory caches and fixed-size layer states. Adapted serving software is required, and the separate inference engine initially supports text alone.

## Session continuation keeps earlier conversation state

The model developer Blockway has released Agens Volundr 32B v1 with a session-continuation feature for long AI agent conversations. The company’s model card describes carrying the state associated with an earlier conversation prefix into the next request. Newly appended messages receive processing on subsequent turns, while the state from earlier input is reused. The release follows the October 5 Preview and includes completed continued pre-training and additional training aimed at extended agent use. [1]

...

## Different layers hold different kinds of memory

Volundr combines layers that retain a growing key-value cache with layers holding a fixed-size state. A key-value cache saves information from earlier input for reuse. Of the model’s 72 layers, 18 retain that growing cache while 54 use fixed-size states. The main model accepts images as well as text. Deployment depends on Blockway’s adapted serving software, making the software path part of using the released weights. [1]

...

## The separate engine initially serves text

Blockway also provides the MIT-licensed Agens Engine for inference, the process of running a trained model to produce output. Its first release supports text only. The engine can move some data into host memory and store weights at different bit widths. The model card separately reports company-run evaluations of repetition and task completion, including some regressions against the Preview on general evaluations. Some tables select the best of several runs; those figures come from the vendor’s testing. [1]

signals.title: NVIDIA Open Sources Run:ai Under Apache 2.0 for Kubernetes GPU Orchestration
signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA Open Sources Run:ai Under Apache 2.0 for Kubernetes GPU Orchestration

By

Asif Razzaq

October 18, 2026

NVIDIA has released the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform as open source software. The source code ships under the Apache 2.0 license on GitHub. NVIDIA Run:ai open source puts production GPU scheduling, quotas and workload management in developers’ hands. The release, makes Run:ai part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. Platform teams can now inspect, fork and self-host the stack without a paid subscription.

## TL;DR

- Size: Monorepo with control plane, cluster services, installer, CLI and MCP server. Local dev builds about 50 Go services.
- Runs on: Kubernetes or OpenShift clusters with NVIDIA GPUs. Local dev runs on macOS or Linux with 8 simulated Tesla-A10 GPUs, no GPU needed.
- Performance: NVIDIA published no platform-level benchmark for this release.
- Best: The related Model Streamer loaded models 3x to 6x faster on 8 NVIDIA H100 VMs on Azure.
- Worst: The community edition has no NVIDIA enterprise support. Local builds need 16 GB RAM and 100 GB disk on Linux.

...

## What is NVIDIA Run:ai?

NVIDIA Run:ai is an AI workload and GPU orchestration platform for Kubernetes from NVIDIA. It schedules development, training and inference workloads across shared GPU clusters. It runs on top of Kubernetes and does not replace it.

The control plane handles workload submission, resource management and monitoring. Cluster services run on each Kubernetes cluster and add GPU-aware scheduling. Users reach it through a web UI, CLI, REST API and an MCP server for AI assistants.

...

## How do developers run NVIDIA Run:ai locally?

The local development guide stands on 1 script, `local-dev.sh`. It builds about 50 Go services from source inside containers. It then creates a 5-node Kind cluster pinned to Kubernetes v1.32.5. A fake GPU operator simulates 8 Tesla-A10 GPUs, so no GPU hardware is required.

- Supported hosts: macOS or Linux, on amd64 or arm64. Windows is not supported.
- Linux hosts need 4 CPUs, 16 GB RAM and 100 GB free disk.
- macOS Podman VMs need at least 12 GB RAM.
- 1 full build leaves about 44 GB of caches.

The `--gpu-operator` flag switches to real NVIDIA GPUs. That mode needs Linux, Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. AMD and Intel accelerators are not supported.

...

## What related open source projects ship alongside?

Two adjacent projects round out the stack. Model Streamer streams model weights directly into GPU memory. vLLM and SGLang enable it with `--load-format runai_streamer`.

Microsoft’s published benchmark used 8 NVIDIA H100 VMs. It showed 3x to 6x faster loading than the default loader. Throughput held at 80 Gbps versus about 40 Gbps on the default path.

Grove orchestrates multicomponent inference workloads. It starts components such as prefill and decode as all-or-nothing units.

signals.title: Tencent Open-Sources Hy Memory 2.0 Stack | Let's Data Science
signals.excerpt:
| October 17, 2026| By LDS Team

Photo: cms-image.pandaily.com · rights & takedowns

Tencent Hunyuan released and open-sourced Hy Memory 2.0 on October 16-17, adding working and code memory to its agent-memory framework. The release includes the Apache 2.0-licensed Hy-Memory-30B-A3B memory writer model, the hy-memory SDK, and the local-first MemHub application. Tencent reports 72.6% LoCoMo accuracy for chat memory while reducing tokens per question from 1,159 to 703.

Tencent Hunyuan has open-sourced Hy Memory 2.0, an agent-memory stack that adds working-memory and code-memory capabilities alongside its existing chat-memory system. The release includes the hy-memory Python SDK, the Hy-Memory-30B-A3B memory writer model, and MemHub, a local-first desktop and command-line application for sharing memory across AI tools.

According to Pandaily, Hy Memory 2.0 manages three distinct memory categories: chat, working, and code. Working memory records task goals, decisions, intermediate results, and reusable lessons with their applicable conditions. Code memory applies a similar persistence layer to software-development tasks, while chat memory groups facts into events involving time, place, and people, then merges duplicates and resolves conflicts before context reaches an answer model.

...

The Hugging Face model card describes Hy-Memory-30B-A3B as a long-term-memory writer intended to replace a general-purpose LLM in the write path of frameworks including Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Its stated role is to decide what information to retain, how to represent it, and how subsequent evidence updates the memory bank.

The model is a mixture-of-experts system with roughly 30 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters, according to Pandaily and the model card. Tencent Hunyuan trained it in two stages: Memory On-Policy Distillation, followed by Attributed Memory Reinforcement Learning. The model card describes the latter as assigning chunk-level credit based on the quality of the resulting memory bank.

...

Tencent's model-card evaluation holds retrieval configuration, prompts, answer model, judge, and other framework components fixed while changing only the memory writer. On a fixed 20% benchmark subsample spanning four memory-framework harnesses, Tencent reports a 55.49 macro average for Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, compared with 54.62 for Claude Opus 5 and 53.64 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

...

Those results are not a blanket claim that the model outperforms every alternative on every task. PC Watch reports that, on Mem0's LoCoMo chat-memory test, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B scored 59.54 versus 69.47 for Claude Opus 5. The reported aggregate advantage therefore depends on the four-harness average and its selected metrics.

...

Pandaily reports separate framework-level results for Hy Memory 2.0, including 72.6% accuracy on LoCoMo for chat memory. It also reports that the framework reduced average tokens per question from 1,159 to 703, a 39.3% decrease. These figures should be distinguished from the writer-model score reported in the cross-framework evaluation, because they cover different configurations and measurement setups.

...

For the new memory types, Pandaily reports a 55.31% average for working memory on MemoryArena travel-planning and shopping tasks. It reports 64.2% question-answering accuracy and 35.6% task resolution on CodeMemoryBench for code memory, plus 28.3% task resolution on SWE-ContextBench.

...

MemHub provides a local store for memory collected from permitted AI tools. PC Watch reports that the app can consolidate conversation histories and work records from tools such as Claude Code and Cursor into a local directory, enabling one tool to reference work previously conducted in another.

...

For practitioners building long-running agents, the notable architectural choice is separation of memory writing from answer generation. Comparable external-memory systems can evaluate retention, update, and conflict-resolution policies independently of the main inference model. That separation can make benchmark interpretation more precise, but teams will still need to test retrieval quality, data-governance controls, and cross-tool memory boundaries in their own agent workflows.

...

- 1 Tencent released an open memory stack spanning SDK, specialized writer model, and local application, enabling modular agent-memory experimentation.
- 2 Hy-Memory-30B-A3B uses about 3B active MoE parameters for memory writing, separating retention decisions from answer-model inference.
- 3 Tencent's reported benchmark gains vary by harness, illustrating why practitioners should compare memory configurations rather than rely on aggregate scores.

...

This is a notable open-source release for teams building persistent AI agents, with a dedicated memory writer, SDK, and local application. Its reported benchmarks and Apache 2.0 licensing make it practically relevant, although the performance claims are vendor-reported and vary across individual harnesses.

candidates.audience_pain: Applying general LLMs to specialized data often yields suboptimal results; need for powerful, targeted AI.
candidates.why_now: Timestral is a recent high-interest announcement from a leading AI company.
candidates.hook_seed: LLMs for *your* data? Mistral's new path.

candidates.topic: Maxwell: New Model Between Code and Hardware
candidates.angle: Introduce Maxwell, a novel model type designed to bridge the gap between high-level code and low-level hardware execution, potentially simplifying and optimizing the deployment of AI systems.
candidates.audience_pain: Complexity and inefficiencies in compiling/running AI models on diverse hardware.
candidates.why_now: Recent announcement and discussion on Hacker News.
candidates.hook_seed: AI's new layer: code to hardware.
